title: Mist
source: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers (Boston: James Munroe, 1849), chapter 'Tuesday' (untitled in the Week; the title 'Mist' was given in Poems of Nature, ed. Salt & Sanborn, 1895)
lines: Low-anchored cloud,
Newfoundland air,
Fountain-head and source of rivers,
Dew-cloth, dream drapery,
And napkin spread by fays;
Drifting meadow of the air,
Where bloom the daisied banks and violets,
And in whose fenny labyrinth
The bittern booms and heron wades;
Spirit of lakes and seas and rivers,
Bear only perfumes and the scent
Of healing herbs to just men’s fields!
notes: Text of A Week (1849), confirmed identically by henrythoreau.org and storyroom.com. These online copies may all come from the same etext, and I did not see a scan of the 1849 first edition. americanliterature.com agrees except 'Fountainhead' (no hyphen). The 1895 Poems of Nature text (Gutenberg #59988, poets.org), which supplies the title 'Mist', differs in three places: 'Dew-cloth, dream-drapery,' / 'Spirit of lakes and seas and rivers,—' / '...just men’s fields.' (full stop, not '!'). Use the 1895 readings if you want to cite it as 'Mist' from Poems of Nature. One stanza, no breaks. In the Week it follows the prose sentence about the morning fog on the Merrimack ('In the present instance it was even fragrant and invigorating, and we enjoyed it as a sort of earlier sunshine…').

title: Inversnaid
source: Poems of Gerard Manley Hopkins, Now First Published, ed. Robert Bridges (London: Humphrey Milford, 1918), no. 33
lines: This darksome burn, horseback brown,
His rollrock highroad roaring down,
In coop and in comb the fleece of his foam
Flutes and low to the lake falls home.
A windpuff-bonnet of fáwn-fróth
Turns and twindles over the broth
Of a pool so pitchblack, féll-frówning,
It rounds and rounds Despair to drowning.
Degged with dew, dappled with dew
Are the groins of the braes that the brook treads through,
Wiry heathpacks, flitches of fern,
And the beadbonny ash that sits over the burn.
What would the world be, once bereft
Of wet and of wildness? Let them be left,
O let them be left, wildness and wet;
Long live the weeds and the wilderness yet.
notes: Gutenberg #22403 (the 1918 Bridges edition) and crossref-it agree word for word. One doubt: both of them came through the fetch tool as 'fáawn-fróth' (an extra 'a'), while poetsgraves gives 'fáwn-fróth'. 'fáawn' is not a word and is almost certainly a combining-accent artefact (a plain 'a' followed by U+0301), so I used 'fáwn-fróth'. Check this one word against a scan of the 1918 page before shipping. The accents are Hopkins's stress marks as printed in 1918. Keep them, or drop all four (fáwn, fróth, féll, frówning) if your font renders them badly. The 1918 text prints the first word as 'THIS' in small capitals (a typographic opening, not part of the wording). The Loyola page has two errors ('rounds and round', 'OF wet') and was not followed. Written 1881.

title: To the Fountain of Bandusia (Odes III.13, 'O fons Bandusiae')
source: The Odes and Carmen Saeculare of Horace, translated into English verse by John Conington (London: Bell and Daldy, 1863; later eds. incl. George Bell & Sons, 1882), Book III, Ode XIII
lines: Bandusia’s fount, in clearness crystalline,
O worthy of the wine, the flowers we vow!
To-morrow shall be thine
A kid, whose crescent brow
Is sprouting all for love and victory.
In vain: his warm red blood, so early stirr’d,
Thy gelid stream shall dye,
Child of the wanton herd.
Thee the fierce Sirian star, to madness fired,
Forbears to touch: sweet cool thy waters yield
To ox with ploughing tired,
And lazy sheep afield.
Thou too one day shalt win proud eminence
’Mid honour’d founts, while I the ilex sing
Crowning the cavern, whence
Thy babbling wavelets spring.
notes: Wording identical in Wikisource and Perseus (Conington, Bell 1882). Small differences: Perseus prints 'Tomorrow' and 'stirr’d.' (full stop). Wikisource prints 'To-morrow' and 'stirr’d,'. I followed Wikisource for both, since the 19th-century spelling is 'To-morrow' and the sense needs a comma ('his warm red blood, so early stirr’d, / Thy gelid stream shall dye'). Neither page showed the stanza breaks clearly. The ode is in four quatrains (long, long, short, short lines), and Perseus breaks after line 4, so I set breaks after lines 4, 8 and 12. Wikisource prints the first word as 'BANDUSIA’S' (a typographic opening). The Gutenberg #5432 file ('Third Edition', no year on the title page) could not be read as far as Book III Ode XIII through the fetch tool.

title: [I built my hut in a zone of human habitation] (Drinking Wine, no. 5)
source: A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems, translated by Arthur Waley (London: Constable and Company, 1918), Chapter III 'Poems by T’ao Ch’ien', no. (7)
lines: I built my hut in a zone of human habitation,
Yet near me there sounds no noise of horse or coach.
Would you know how that is possible?
A heart that is distant creates a wilderness round it.
I pluck chrysanthemums under the eastern hedge,
Then gaze long at the distant summer hills.
The mountain air is fresh at the dusk of day:
The flying birds two by two return.
In these things there lies a deep meaning;
Yet when we would express it, words suddenly fail us.
notes: Three copies agree exactly (Gutenberg HTML, the old Gutenberg plain text, and a substack that cites Waley 1918). Waley prints no title, only the number (7) under 'Poems by T’ao Ch’ien', and no footnote. It is the fifth of the 'Drinking Wine' poems, but Waley does not say so, so the bracketed title is mine. The Li Po alternate was not needed. (Waley's 1919 More Translations from the Chinese has no T’ao Ch’ien.)

title: I Saw in Louisiana a Live-Oak Growing
source: Leaves of Grass (Philadelphia: David McKay, 1891-92), 'Calamus', p. 106 (final 'deathbed' text)
lines: I saw in Louisiana a live-oak growing,
All alone stood it and the moss hung down from the branches,
Without any companion it grew there uttering joyous leaves of dark green,
And its look, rude, unbending, lusty, made me think of myself,
But I wonder’d how it could utter joyous leaves standing alone there without its friend near, for I knew I could not,
And I broke off a twig with a certain number of leaves upon it, and twined around it a little moss,
And brought it away, and I have placed it in sight in my room,
It is not needed to remind me as of my own dear friends,
(For I believe lately I think of little else than of them,)
Yet it remains to me a curious token, it makes me think of manly love;
For all that, and though the live-oak glistens there in Louisiana solitary in a wide flat space,
Uttering joyous leaves all its life without a friend a lover near,
I know very well I could not.
notes: This is the 1891-92 text (the same as 1881-82). The Whitman Archive 1891-92 and 1881-82 transcriptions and the Poetry Foundation (source note 'Leaves of Grass (1891-2)') agree word for word. The Archive breaks long lines to match the printed page, but these are not separate verse lines. One stanza. The 1891 edition prints 'I SAW' in capitals, which is typographic. The 1867 text punctuates differently (see the alternate below). The poem first appeared in 1860 as 'Calamus' no. 20.

alternates.label: 1867 text (Leaves of Grass, New York, 1867), single source: Whitman Archive LG/1867/poems/37
alternates.title: I saw in Louisiana a Live-Oak Growing.
lines: I saw in Louisiana a live-oak growing,
All alone stood it, and the moss hung down from the branches;
Without any companion it grew there, uttering joyous leaves of dark green,
And its look, rude, unbending, lusty, made me think of myself;
But I wonder’d how it could utter joyous leaves, standing alone there, without its friend, its lover near—for I knew I could not;
And I broke off a twig with a certain number of leaves upon it, and twined around it a little moss,
And brought it away—and I have placed it in sight in my room;
It is not needed to remind me as of my own dear friends,
(For I believe lately I think of little else than of them;)
Yet it remains to me a curious token—it makes me think of manly love;
—For all that, and though the live-oak glistens there in Louisiana, solitary, in a wide flat space,
Uttering joyous leaves all its life, without a friend, a lover, near,
I know very well I could not.

title: Chien Chia (Reed and Rush) — Odes of Ch’in, IV (Shijing: Jian jia)
source: The She King; or, The Book of Ancient Poetry, translated in English verse by James Legge (London: Trübner, 1876), Book XI (The Odes of Ch’in), IV. Text as reproduced verbatim in The Book of Poetry (Shanghai: Chinese Book Co., 1931) and transcribed at sacred-texts.com
lines: Reed and rush are dark and green;
As hoarfrost the white dew is seen.
Him, the man I have in mind,
By this water I should find.
Searching, up the stream I haste,
On a long and toilsome quest.
Downwards then I turn, and see!
In the midstream standeth he.
He is there but far removed;
Vain has all my searching proved.
Reed and rush luxuriant rise;
Still undried the white dew lies.
Him, the man I have in mind,
On the stream’s edge I should find.
Upwards first my course I keep,
Though the way is rough and steep.
Downwards then, and what to see?
In the midstream standeth he,
On the islet, far removed;—
Vain has all my searching proved.
Reed and rush grow thick and tall;
Ceases not the dew to fall.
Him, the man I have in mind,
On the stream’s bank I should find.
Upwards first I go along,
But the hard path leads me wrong.
Downwards then my steps I turn,
And in midstream him discern,
On the island, far removed;—
Vain has all my searching proved.
notes: This is Legge's 1876 rhymed version (not the 1871 Chinese Classics or 1879 SBE prose). sacred-texts says the 1931 Shanghai reprint 'contains the poetry verbatim from the 1876 edition'. Two fetches (sacred-texts.com and its neonvagabond mirror) agree exactly, but the mirror is the same transcription, so this is not an independent second source. Hence verified_two_sources is false. No other online copy of the 1876 verse text turned up. Legge's headnote, printed above the poem: 'The Chien Chia; narrative. Some one tells how he sought another, whom it seemed easy to find, and yet could not find him.' Suggested excerpt: stanza 1 (10 lines), or stanzas 1-2 (indices 0-20, 20 lines). The Jennings (1891) and Allen (1891) versions were not checked. The Basho/Chamberlain alternate could not be verified, because no reachable page quoted Chamberlain's 1902 renderings.

title: To a Waterfowl
source: Poems by William Cullen Bryant, Authorized Edition (Dessau: Katz Brothers, 1854) [Gutenberg #16341]; first printed in the North American Review, March 1818; collected in Poems (1821)
lines: Whither, midst falling dew,
While glow the heavens with the last steps of day,
Far, through their rosy depths, dost thou pursue
Thy solitary way?
Vainly the fowler’s eye
Might mark thy distant flight to do thee wrong,
As, darkly painted on the crimson sky,
Thy figure floats along.
Seek’st thou the plashy brink
Of weedy lake, or marge of river wide,
Or where the rocking billows rise and sink
On the chafed ocean side?
There is a Power whose care
Teaches thy way along that pathless coast,—
The desert and illimitable air,—
Lone wandering, but not lost.
All day thy wings have fanned,
At that far height, the cold, thin atmosphere,
Yet stoop not, weary, to the welcome land,
Though the dark night is near.
And soon that toil shall end;
Soon shalt thou find a summer home, and rest,
And scream among thy fellows; reeds shall bend,
Soon, o’er thy sheltered nest.
Thou’rt gone, the abyss of heaven
Hath swallowed up thy form; yet, on my heart
Deeply hath sunk the lesson thou hast given,
And shall not soon depart.
He who, from zone to zone,
Guides through the boundless sky thy certain flight,
In the long way that I must tread alone,
Will lead my steps aright.
notes: This is the 1854 Authorized Edition text (Gutenberg #16341). A line-by-line comparison against literarydevices.net found the same wording, with two exceptions: literarydevices drops the dashes after 'coast,' and 'air,' (Gutenberg and VCU both have them), and prints 'Seekst' (a typo; every other source has 'Seek’st'). The 1880 Household Edition (Gutenberg #29700, Bryant's late revision), also matched by all-creatures.org, differs in four places: line 7 'As, darkly seen against the crimson sky,' / line 12 'On the chafed ocean-side?' / lines 14-15 'coast—' and 'air—' (no comma) / line 27 'Deeply has sunk the lesson'. VCU and discoverpoetry print an early form ''midst' with an apostrophe, and discoverpoetry has several other errors. Excerpt: stanzas 1-4 (16 lines, indices 0-18), or stanzas 1-4 plus 7-8 for 24 lines with the ending (excerpt_ranges).

title: Fragments of Herakleitos
source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy, 2nd ed. (London: Adam and Charles Black, 1908), ch. III, §65 'The Fragments' (Bywater's numbering, as used by Burnet)

fragments.text: You cannot step twice into the same rivers; for fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you.
We step and do not step into the same rivers; we are and are not.
The sun is new every day.
The way up and the way down is one and the same.
All things are an exchange for Fire, and Fire for all things, even as wares for gold and gold for wares.
Fire lives the death of air, and air lives the death of fire; water lives the death of earth, earth that of water.
Even the posset separates if it is not stirred.
Time is a child playing draughts, the kingly power is a child’s.

lines: (41, 42) You cannot step twice into the same rivers; for fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you.
(81) We step and do not step into the same rivers; we are and are not.
(32) The sun is new every day.
(10) Nature loves to hide.
(69) The way up and the way down is one and the same.
(22) All things are an exchange for Fire, and Fire for all things, even as wares for gold and gold for wares.
(25) Fire lives the death of air, and air lives the death of fire; water lives the death of earth, earth that of water.
(84) Even the posset separates if it is not stirred.
(79) Time is a child playing draughts, the kingly power is a child’s.
notes: Fordham (which names the 1908 2nd ed., pp. 146-156) and the spbu PDF of ch. III (edition not stated, but it cites 'the first edition', so it is the 2nd or 3rd) agree exactly on all nine fragments. Burnet prints each number in parentheses before the fragment, as here. A footnote marker after 'air' in (25) is omitted. The order is thematic (river first), not Burnet's. I left out fr. (20), the 'ever-living Fire', because the two sources differ: 1908/Fordham reads 'This world (kosmos), which is the same for all, no one of gods or men has made; but it was ever, is now, and ever shall be an ever-living Fire, with measures kindling, and measures going out.' The spbu copy reads '...with measures of it kindling, and measures going out' and has no '(kosmos)'. That is probably the 1920 revision. Pick one edition if you want it. Burnet's 1892 1st edition was not checked; its numbering is also Bywater's, but its wording may differ.

title: The Flood (Epic of Gilgamish, Tablet XI, ll. 97-154)
poet: Epic of Gilgamesh (Standard Babylonian / Assyrian version)
source: The Epic of Gilgamish: A New Translation from a Collation of the Cuneiform Tablets in the British Museum Rendered Literally into English Hexameters, by R. Campbell Thompson (London: Luzac, 1928), Eleventh Tablet
lines: (Then), when something of dawn had appear’d, from out the horizon
Rose a cloud darkling; (lo), Adad (the storm-god) was rumbling within it,
Nabu and Sharru were leading the vanguard, and coming as heralds
Over the hills and the levels: (then) Irragal wrench’d out the bollards;
Havoc Ninurta let loose as he came, th’ Anunnaki their torches
Brandish’d, and shrivell’d the land with their flames; desolation from Adad
Stretch’d to (high) Heaven, (and) all that was bright was turn’d into darkness.
Nor could a brother distinguish his brother; from heaven were mortals
Not to be spied. O, were stricken with terror the gods at the Deluge,
Fleeing, they rose to the Heaven of Anu, and crouch’d in the outskirts,
Cow’ring like curs were the gods (while) like to a woman in travail
Ishtar did cry, she shrieking aloud, (e’en) the sweet-spoken Lady
(She of the gods): ‘May that day turn to dust, because I spake evil
(There) in th’ Assemblage of Gods! O, how could I utter (such) evil
(There) in the Assemblage of Gods, (so) to blot out my people, ordaining
Havoc! Sooth, then, am I to give birth, unto (these) mine own people
Only to glut (with their bodies) the Sea as though they were fish-spawn?’
Gods—Anunnaki—wept with her, the gods were sitting (all) humbled,
(Aye), in (their) weeping, (and) closed were their lips ⌜amid (?)⌝ the Assemblage.
Six days, a se’nnight the hurricane, deluge, (and) tempest continued
Sweeping the land: when the seventh day came, were quelléd the warfare,
Tempest (and) deluge which like to an army embattail’d were fighting.
Lull’d was the sea, (all) spent was the gale, assuaged was the deluge,
(So) did I look on the day; (lo), sound was (all) still’d; and all human
Back to (its) clay was return’d, and fen was level with roof-tree.
(Then) I open’d a hatchway, and down on my cheek stream’d the sunlight,
Bowing myself, I sat weeping, my tears o’er my cheek(s) overflowing,
Into the distance I gazed, to the furthest bounds of the Ocean,
Land was uprear’d at twelve (points), and the Ark on the Mountain of Nisir
Grounded; the Mountain of Nisir held fast, nor gave lease to her shifting.
One day, (nay,) two, did Nisir hold fast, nor give lease to her shifting.
Three days, (nay), four, did Nisir hold fast, nor give lease to her shifting,
Five days, (nay,) six, did Nisir hold fast, nor give lease to her shifting.
(Then), when the seventh day dawn’d, I put forth a dove, and released (her),
(But) to and fro went the dove, and return’d (for) a resting-place was not.
(Then) I a swallow put forth and released; to and fro went the swallow,
She (too) return’d, (for) a resting-place was not; I put forth a raven,
Her, (too,) releasing; the raven went, too, and th’ abating of waters
Saw; and she ate as she waded (and) splash’d, (unto me) not returning.
notes: Every line was confirmed in both sources (sacred-texts and americanliterature 'Original Text'; a row-by-row comparison found all wording identical). Thompson's line numbers are left out: index 0 = l. 97, 'Nabu and Sharru' = 100, 'Brandish’d' = 105, 'Cow’ring' = 115, '(There) in th’ Assemblage' = 120, 'Gods—Anunnaki' = 125, 'Tempest (and) deluge' = 130, hatchway = 135, 'Land was uprear’d' = 140, dove = 145, swallow = 150. The gaps in the numbering are Thompson's own; he numbers by tablet line. The blank entry at index 7 stands for Thompson's editorial note, which is not verse: '(Four lines mutilated "the land like . . .," "for one day the st[orm] . . .," "fiercely blew . . . ." "like a battle . . .").' Source differences: (1) Index 19: americanliterature has half-brackets '⌜amid (?)⌝'. sacred-texts has 'amid(?)]the', which has lost the opening bracket. Thompson marks restorations with half-brackets, so I followed americanliterature. If your font lacks ⌜⌝, plain [ ] is acceptable but less faithful. (2) Ishtar's speech: sacred-texts uses single quotes ‘…’, americanliterature uses double “…”. I followed sacred-texts, the transcription of the book, and made them curly. Footnote markers are omitted (sacred-texts footnote on 'a se’nnight': 'Lit. "and."'). Suggested excerpts: contiguous 20 lines (indices 20-39: six days, calm, hatchway, Nisir, the dove, swallow and raven), or 21 lines with elisions (excerpt_ranges: storm rising 0-6, gods weeping and humbled, six days and the calm 18-25, the birds 34-39). Each range starts and ends at a sentence boundary. The 'gods cowering like curs' passage (indices 9-17) is one long sentence that runs into Ishtar's speech, so it cannot be cut short. Take all of it or none.

title: Song IX. Invocation. (Consolation of Philosophy, Book III, Metre 9)
source: The Consolation of Philosophy of Boethius, translated into English prose and verse by H. R. James (London: Elliot Stock, 1897), Book III, Song IX
lines: Maker of earth and sky, from age to age
Who rul’st the world by reason; at whose word
Time issues from Eternity’s abyss:
To all that moves the source of movement, fixed
Thyself and moveless. Thee no cause impelled
Extrinsic this proportioned frame to shape
From shapeless matter; but, deep-set within
Thy inmost being, the form of perfect good,
From envy free; and Thou didst mould the whole
To that supernal pattern. Beauteous
The world in Thee thus imaged, being Thyself
Most beautiful. So Thou the work didst fashion
In that fair likeness, bidding it put on
Perfection through the exquisite perfectness
Of every part’s contrivance. Thou dost bind
The elements in balanced harmony,
So that the hot and cold, the moist and dry,
Contend not; nor the pure fire leaping up
Escape, or weight of waters whelm the earth.
Thou joinest and diffusest through the whole,
Linking accordantly its several parts,
A soul of threefold nature, moving all.
This, cleft in twain, and in two circles gathered,
Speeds in a path that on itself returns,
Encompassing mind’s limits, and conforms
The heavens to her true semblance. Lesser souls
And lesser lives by a like ordinance
Thou sendest forth, each to its starry car
Affixing, and dost strew them far and wide
O’er earth and heaven. These by a law benign
Thou biddest turn again, and render back
To thee their fires. Oh, grant, almighty Father,
Grant us on reason’s wing to soar aloft
To heaven’s exalted height; grant us to see
The fount of good; grant us, the true light found,
To fix our steadfast eyes in vision clear
On Thee. Disperse the heavy mists of earth,
And shine in Thine own splendour. For Thou art
The true serenity and perfect rest
Of every pious soul—to see Thy face,
The end and the beginning—One the guide,
The traveller, the pathway, and the goal.
notes: IMPORTANT: James's version does NOT open 'O Thou who dost by everlasting reason rule'. That line is not in his text (it may come from another translation or a paraphrase). James's Song IX opens 'Maker of earth and sky, from age to age'. The full text came from Poetry Chaikhana ('English version by H. R. James'). A word-by-word comparison against Monadnock Valley Press's transcription matched all 42 lines, except that Monadnock spaces the two em dashes (' — '). Both have lower-case 'thee' in 'To thee their fires.' The fetch tool would not read past Book III ch. VIII in any copy of the 1897 book (Gutenberg #14328, archive.org), so the printed edition itself was not checked. Stanza breaks: both sources break after line 19. Monadnock also shows a blank line after line 11 ('being Thyself' / 'Most beautiful.'), which falls mid-sentence and is probably a page-break artefact, so I left it out. Excerpts: lines 20-42 (world-soul, souls set on starry cars, prayer; 23 lines) suit the trestle under the stars. Lines 1-19 (index 0-18; the Timaeus creation and the elements bound in harmony) are the other complete verse paragraph.

title: To Stella (From the Greek of Plato)
source: Poetical Works of Percy Bysshe Shelley, ed. Mrs. Shelley (London: Moxon, 1839), 1st ed.; text as in Complete Poetical Works, ed. Thomas Hutchinson (Oxford, 1904/1914), 'Epigrams', no. 1
lines: Thou wert the morning star among the living,
Ere thy fair light had fled;—
Now, having died, thou art as Hesperus, giving
New splendour to the dead.
notes: Four sources agree exactly. Shelley's title as printed by Hutchinson is '1.—TO STELLA.' with the subheading 'FROM THE GREEK OF PLATO.' Hutchinson's note: 'These four Epigrams were published—numbers 2 and 4 without title—by Mrs. Shelley, "Poetical Works", 1839, 1st edition.' So 'To Stella' was published under that title in 1839 and its title is Shelley's (or Mary Shelley's). The other three epigrams are 'Kissing Helena', 'Spirit of Plato' and 'Circumstance'. A pre-1929 alternative for the same epigram is Rennell Rodd, 'The Unset Star' (Love, Worship and Death, 1916): 'Star that didst on the living at dawn thy lustre shed, / Now as the star of evening thou shinest with the dead!' (Gutenberg #35907 and Yandex Books, which is probably a copy of the same file).

title: Starworship
source: Rennell Rodd, Love, Worship and Death: Some Renderings from the Greek Anthology (London: Edward Arnold, 1916), 'Plato', II
lines: Thou gazest starward, star of mine, whose heaven I fain would be,
That all my myriad starry eyes might only gaze on thee.
notes: Shelley did not translate this epigram, as far as I can confirm. Hutchinson's Complete Poetical Works has only four Plato-derived epigrams, and this is not one of them; 'myriad eyes' appears nowhere in Gutenberg #4799. Wikiquote credits a five-line 'Aster' to Shelley, Poetical Works (1839): 'Thou gazest on the stars: / Would I might be, / O star of mine, the skies / With myriad eyes / To gaze on thee.' poetryexplorer.net prints the same lines with no translator. Treat that attribution as doubtful and don't print it as Shelley's without checking a facsimile of Mrs. Shelley's 1839 volume. Rodd's 1916 verse is used here. Gutenberg #35907 and Yandex Books agree, but Yandex is probably built from the Gutenberg file, so verified_two_sources is false. Other pre-1929 versions found, none verified from a primary copy: (1) J. W. Mackail, Select Epigrams (1890), prose, quoted on a MobileRead forum post: 'On the stars thou gazest, my Star; would I were heaven, that I might look on thee with many eyes.' (2) W. R. Paton, Greek Anthology (Loeb, vol. II, 1917), prose. Wikipedia 'Epigrams (Plato)' gives, unattributed but almost certainly Paton's wording: 'Thou lookest on the stars, my Star. Would I were heaven, to look on thee with many eyes.' attalus.org prints the same in modernised form ('You look on the stars, my Star. Would I were heaven, to look on you with many eyes.'). (3) G. B. Grundy, Ancient Gems in Modern Settings (1913), via Wikiquote only: 'My star, thou gazest on the stars: O would that I might be / The starry sky, so gaze might I with myriad eyes on thee!' The 7.669 text in Gutenberg's Mackail (#2378) could not be reached; the readable portion is the Introduction.

title: Greek Anthology XVI.13 (Planudean Appendix), attributed to Plato
source: The Greek Anthology, with an English translation by W. R. Paton, Loeb Classical Library (London: Heinemann; New York: Putnam, 1916-18), vol. V, Book XVI, no. 13
lines: Sit down by this high-foliaged vocal pine that quivers in the constant western breeze, and beside my plashing stream Pan’s pipe shall bring slumber to thy charmed eyelids.
notes: This is Paton's prose (ToposText, which credits Paton's public-domain Loeb text). Wikipedia's 'Epigrams (Plato)' gives the identical wording, unattributed. attalus.org has the same, modernised to 'your charmed eyelids'. Mackail's 1890 version could not be checked, because the epigram section of Gutenberg #2378 was out of the fetch tool's reach. Paton's Book XVI is in Loeb vol. V; I believe that volume came out in 1918, but I did not confirm the date. Paton's whole set is 1916-18, so it is pre-1929 in any case.

title: Tao Te Ching, ch. 8 (opening)
source: The Texts of Taoism, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 39; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1891), Tâo Teh King, ch. 8
lines: The highest excellence is like (that of) water. The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving (to the contrary), the low place which all men dislike.
notes: Gutenberg #216 and sacred-texts (SBE 39, 1891) agree exactly. Legge's parentheses mark words he supplied; keep them. The chapter continues: 'Hence (its way) is near to (that of) the Tâo.' I did not verify that sentence word by word.

title: Tao Te Ching, ch. 78 (opening)
source: The Texts of Taoism, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 39, 1891), Tâo Teh King, ch. 78
lines: There is nothing in the world more soft and weak than water, and yet for attacking things that are firm and strong there is nothing that can take precedence of it;—for there is nothing (so effectual) for which it can be changed.
Every one in the world knows that the soft overcomes the hard, and the weak the strong, but no one is able to carry it out in practice.
notes: Both sources agree. Gutenberg prints the dash as an em dash (';—for'); sacred-texts' plain text shows it as '--'. Excerpt: the first sentence alone is a good commonplace entry, or use both.

title: Zhuangzi, Book XVII, Khiû Shui, or 'The Floods of Autumn' (opening)
source: The Texts of Taoism, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 39, 1891), The Writings of Kwang-dze, Book XVII
lines: The time of the autumnal floods was come, and the hundred streams were all discharging themselves into the Ho.
notes: sacred-texts (SBE 39) and the NTUST page, which quotes the same sentence without naming a translator, agree. Legge's page header is 'BOOK XVII. PART II. SECTION X. Khiû Shui, or "The Floods of Autumn."' Herbert Giles's 1889 version (Gutenberg #59709) was out of the fetch tool's reach and was not checked.

title: Zhuangzi, Book XVII: Kwang-dze and Hui-dze on the dam over the Hâo
source: The Texts of Taoism, Part I (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 39, 1891), The Writings of Kwang-dze, Book XVII, par. 13
lines: Kwang-dze and Hui-dze were walking on the dam over the Hâo, when the former said, ‘These thryssas come out, and play about at their ease;—that is the enjoyment of fishes.’
The other said, ‘You are not a fish; how do you know what constitutes the enjoyment of fishes?’
Kwang-dze rejoined, ‘You are not I. How do you know that I do not know what constitutes the enjoyment of fishes?’
Hui-dze said, ‘I am not you; and though indeed I do not fully know you, you certainly are not a fish, and (the argument) is complete against your knowing what constitutes the happiness of fishes.’

Kwang-dze replied, ‘Let us keep to your original question. You said to me, “How do you know what constitutes the enjoyment of fishes?” You knew that I knew it, and yet you put your question to me;—well, I know it (from our enjoying ourselves together) over the Hâo.’
notes: Single source (sacred-texts SBE 39). Two separate fetches agreed on every word. sacred-texts' '--' is printed here as an em dash, and its straight quotes as curly ones. A footnote marker and a page break (p. 392) are omitted. A second pre-1929 version, also verified only on sacred-texts, is Lionel Giles, Musings of a Chinese Mystic (London: John Murray, Wisdom of the East, 1906), based on Herbert Giles's 1889 translation (the page itself does not say so): 'Chuang Tzŭ and Hui Tzŭ had strolled on to the bridge over the Hao, when the former observed: “See how the minnows are darting about! That is the pleasure of fishes.” “You not being a fish yourself,” said Hui Tzŭ, “how can you possibly know in what consists the pleasure of fishes?” “And you not being I,” retorted Chuang Tzŭ, “how can you know that I do not know?” “If I, not being you, cannot know what you know,” urged Hui Tzŭ, “it follows that you, not being a fish, cannot know in what consists the pleasure of fishes.” “Let us go back,” said Chuang Tzŭ, “to your original question. You asked me how I knew in what consists the pleasure of fishes. Your very question shows that you knew I knew. I knew it from my own feelings on this bridge.”' (The model returned the quotation marks inconsistently, so check them before use.) Giles's version reads better as a commonplace entry. Suggested excerpt from Legge: the first three sentences.

title: Empedokles, fragment (6): the four roots
source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy, 2nd ed. (London: A. & C. Black, 1908), ch. V, fr. 6
lines: Hear first the four roots of all things: shining Zeus, life-bringing Hera, Aidoneus, and Nestis whose tear-drops are a well-spring to mortals.
notes: Fordham (1908 2nd ed.) and the spbu PDF (edition unknown) agree on every word, but not on one comma. Fordham has 'Aidoneus, and Nestis'. In spbu, fr. (6) reads 'Aidoneus and Nestis', though spbu's own §107 quotes the line with the comma. I kept the comma (1908). Burnet prints it as prose with the number '(6)' and the cross-reference 'R. P. 164'. The ellopos.net version ('Hear first of all what are the root principles of all things...') is a different, uncredited translation.

title: Xenophanes on fossils (Hippolytus, Ref. i. 14)
source: John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy, ch. II, §59 'Earth and Water' (2nd ed. 1908 or 3rd ed. 1920; the copy read does not say which)
lines: Xenophanes said that a mixture of the earth with the sea is taking place, and that it is being gradually dissolved by the moisture. He says that he has the following proofs of this.

Shells are found in midland districts and on hills, and he says that in the quarries at Syracuse has been found the imprint of a fish and of seaweed, at Paros the form of a bayleaf in the depth of the stone, and at Malta flat impressions of all marine animals.

These, he says, were produced when all things were formerly mud, and the outlines were dried in the mud. All human beings are destroyed when the earth has been carried down into the sea and turned to mud. This change takes place for all the worlds.—Hipp. Ref. i. 14 (R. P. 103 a).
notes: Single source: the spbu PDF of Burnet ch. II. It was read row by row, and nothing appeared to be missing between rows. 'bayleaf' may be 'bay-leaf' in print (unconfirmed). Burnet says 'Malta' where other translations say 'Melite'. Gutenberg's Burnet (#67097, 1908) only refers forward to '§ 59' ('even Xenophanes supported one of his theories by referring to the fossils and petrifactions of such widely separated places as Malta, Paros, and Syracuse', Introduction §XIII); the fetch tool could not reach §59 itself. Alternatives: (1) J. H. MacMahon's Hippolytus, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 5 (1868/1886), Refutation I.xii, confirmed by ccel.org and intratext/bkv: 'that in the midst of earth, and in mountains, shells are discovered; and also in Syracuse he affirms was found in the quarries the print of a fish and of seals, and in Paros an image of a laurel in the bottom of a stone, and in Melita parts of all sorts of marine animals.' (2) Arthur Fairbanks, The First Philosophers of Greece (1898), p. 83, quoted by todayinsci.com: '...that shells are found in the midst of the land and among the mountains, that in the quarries of Syracuse the imprints of a fish and of seals had been found...'. Suggested commonplace line: the middle sentence (index 1).

title: Gilgamish and the serpent (Tablet XI, ll. 285-290)
source: The Epic of Gilgamish, tr. R. Campbell Thompson (London: Luzac, 1928), Eleventh Tablet, 'The Quest ends in Tragedy'
lines: Gilgamish spied out a pool of cool water, (and) therein descending
Bathed in the water. (But here was) a serpent who snuff’d the plant’s fragrance,
Darted he up ⌜from the water (?)⌝, and snatch’d the plant, uttering malison
As he drew back. Then Gilgamish sate him, (and) burst into weeping.
notes: Both sources agree word for word. In line 3, sacred-texts uses square brackets '[from the water (?)]' and americanliterature uses half-brackets ⌜…⌝; Thompson marks restorations with half-brackets. NOTE: Thompson's 1928 text does not mention the snake shedding its skin. That detail is not in his rendering of these lines or in his footnotes, so the game shouldn't attribute 'sloughed its skin' to this translation. The next line reads 'Over his cheeks flow’d his tears: to the boatman Ur-Shanabi [spake he(?)]', which sacred-texts prints as 'Ur -Shanabi' (an OCR space); only its first half was confirmed on americanliterature.
